archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, new regime)
archetype.definition: A first-year Hafley team with Malik Willis at quarterback, a run-heavy plan and a defense that can't rush the passer, playing like the league's worst side while it looks for a foundation.

report.headline: Last in net EPA and earning it; the run game is the only thing working.
report.take:
Miami is 0-5 under first-year coach Jeff Hafley, and the record is not bad luck. The Dolphins are last in net EPA and last in point differential at -12.4 a game. Their wins over expected of -1.15 means the scoreboard says they deserved about one win, not three. Malik Willis has started every game. The bigger picture is a slide that began last year: 2025 was already 27th in net EPA, and the defense ranked 25th then too. This is a franchise in the early, ugly stage of a rebuild, not a good roster having a bad month.

The identity is clear. Miami passes less than expected more than almost anyone (-11.1 pass rate over expected, 31st), and the run game has grown into the offense's one real weapon. Rushing yards went 74, 102, 119, 121, then 217 against Cincinnati, and rush EPA turned positive in each of the last two games. The passing game has moved the other way. Pass EPA was -12.4 at Minnesota and -11.4 against Cincinnati. Willis holds the ball longer than any quarterback in the league, which helps explain a protection unit that is 27th in both pressure rate and sack rate. On defense, the base is sound: the Dolphins rank 3rd in missed-tackle rate and are mid-pack against the run. But they have four sacks in five games, rank 30th in pass EPA allowed and let opponents convert 51.7% on third down. Tight ends have shredded them; the TE1 EPA allowed ranks dead last.

Two things in the numbers deserve context. First, the schedule: four of the five opponents now rank 11th or better in defensive EPA, including Minnesota (1st) and San Francisco (4th). The 14 points a game partly reflects who they played. Second, the 26.4 points allowed overstates how bad the defense is. Miami has eight giveaways against four takeaways, and its special teams lose 3.58 EPA a game (30th), so opponents keep starting with short fields. Yards allowed ranks 18th, well ahead of points allowed at 24th. The pass defense is genuinely bad. The overall defense is merely below average, with the field-position math making it look worse.

The direction is mildly encouraging. The last two losses came by 5 and 7 with a cover and a push, and they came from leaning on the run. The ceiling depends on whether Willis can make the passing game merely functional. Until he does, good run defenses will be able to shut the offense down entirely.

strengths.title: A run game that's finally producing
strengths.body: Rush EPA went from negative in each of the first three games to +4.9 and +9.0 over the last two, capped by 217 yards against Cincinnati. The line creates space early, ranking 9th in yards before contact, and De'Von Achane's return to the backfield alongside Ollie Gordon II adds juice. The weakness is the 29th-ranked stuff rate, so the production is boom-or-bust rather than steady. It should hold against average fronts but is vulnerable against good ones.

strengths.title: Sound tackling, respectable run defense
strengths.body: Miami misses tackles less often than all but two teams, and that discipline keeps its run defense middle of the pack by EPA. That skill is repeatable rather than random. It is why the yardage totals look far more normal than the points allowed.

concerns.title: The passing game has collapsed
concerns.body: Pass EPA has been deeply negative in four of five games, with the last two the worst of the season. Willis holds the ball longer than anyone and the line ranks 27th in sack rate, so drives die on sacks and long-yardage downs. Some of this is a brutal slate of pass defenses. But the trend line is getting worse, not better, and it is the biggest real flaw on the roster.

concerns.title: No pass rush, no third-down stops
concerns.body: Four sacks in five games puts Miami 31st, and without pressure the coverage gives up a 51.7% conversion rate on third down. Tight ends have been the easiest target in the league against this defense. With Storm Duck and Reese Taylor out and JuJu Brents and Michael Taaffe banged up, the secondary is getting thinner, so this is more likely to persist than to fix itself.

concerns.title: Hidden yardage keeps leaking
concerns.body: Special teams cost 3.58 EPA a game (30th), and the -0.8 turnover margin hands opponents short fields. Together these push points allowed well beyond what the defense's yardage suggests. Turnover margin tends to drift toward even, but special-teams problems usually reflect personnel and can linger.

trend.note: The losing margins went -14, -22, -14, -5, -7, with the last two coming against top-11 defenses on the back of a surging run game. The passing game deteriorated over the same stretch, so the improvement is narrow and fragile.

nextGame.headline: Jets' top-seven run defense takes away Miami's only working weapon.
nextGame.body:
The Jets are a bad matchup for how Miami wins. Their defense ranks 7th in EPA overall and 7th against the run, so the ground game that carried the last two weeks runs into the strength of this unit. They also sack quarterbacks on 9.1% of dropbacks (2nd), facing a passer who holds the ball longest in the league. One wrinkle: the Jets get those sacks despite a 30th-ranked pressure rate, which suggests some of it comes from quarterbacks holding on too long. Willis fits that description. On the other side, New York's offense is ordinary (20th in EPA), its line allows sacks at the league's 30th-ranked rate, and it scores 18.6 a game. That gives Miami's defense a playable game, but the Dolphins' four sacks in five games suggest they won't exploit that line.

Availability leans slightly Miami's way only because of the bye: the Dolphins come in on 14 days' rest. Their secondary is still the worry. Storm Duck and Reese Taylor are out, Brents (stinger) and the every-down safety Taaffe (chest) are questionable, and starting guard Jonah Savaiinaea is questionable too. Their return estimates land on game day, so they are uncertain rather than likely. For New York, Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell and guard Dylan Parham were ruled out with return estimates a week before this game, so they may be back. Braiden McGregor is on IR, and tight end Kenyon Sadiq is in the concussion protocol.

keyMatchups.title: Willis' clock vs. Jets' sack rate
keyMatchups.body: Miami's long time to throw meets a defense that finishes plays at an elite rate. If Willis keeps holding the ball, drive-killing sacks are likely. That would push Miami into the long-yardage passing downs where its offense has been worst.

keyMatchups.title: Miami's run game vs. stout front
keyMatchups.body: The Dolphins' recent surge came against Minnesota and Cincinnati. The Jets allow far less on the ground by EPA. Miami's 29th-ranked stuff rate suggests it can be shut down by a front that wins at the line.

keyMatchups.title: Where Miami can throw: the slot
keyMatchups.body: The Jets have been the stingiest team in the league against tight ends, which takes Greg Dulcich away, but they rank 29th against the third receiver. Kevin Coleman Jr. and Chris Bell are the likely beneficiaries if Miami is forced to pass, with Caleb Douglas out.

nextGame.watch: Whether Miami can stay ahead of the chains on early-down runs. If the Jets stuff those runs and force Willis into obvious passing downs, his sack and turnover problems take over the game.

restOfSeason.body:
There is real football left to improve on, and the schedule offers some winnable spots: Indianapolis (22nd offense, 26th defense), the winless Chargers with the league's worst offense, and two Jets games. It also brings Buffalo twice and Detroit, all with top-three offenses that will test a pass defense ranked 30th. The run game and tackling are sustainable. The turnover margin should drift toward even, which will trim points allowed a little. The pass rush and the special teams look structural.

The most likely outcome is a team that stays competitive on the scoreboard more often than in the first three weeks and steals a few games, finishing near the bottom of the league. A genuine turnaround requires the passing game to rise from catastrophic to merely below average. Nothing in the Minnesota and Cincinnati games suggests that is close.

bets.reason: Willis holds the ball longest in the league behind a line ranked 27th in sack rate, facing a Jets defense 2nd in sack rate. Miami has allowed 14 sacks already, including five, four and three in separate games. No line is posted yet, so take this only if the number is set at or near his season average.

Miami averages about 170 passing yards a game, with 85 and 137 in the last two, and passes far less than expected. A Jets pass rush that finishes plays should keep volume and efficiency down. The one risk is the Jets' weakness against third receivers, if Miami falls behind and has to throw.

confidence.note: Five games under a new staff, but the bottom-tier efficiency is consistent across every game.
